Calcium Silicate Hydrate Colloid at Different Humidities: Microstructure, Deformation Mechanism, and Mechanical Properties Chengyao Liang1, Qi Zheng1,2, Jinyang Jiang2, Paulo JM Monteiro1, Shaofan Li1*

1 Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720, United States 2 School of Materials Science and Engineering, Southeast University, Nanjing 211189, P.R. China

* Corresponding authors: Shaofan Li Abstract Calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H) is the main hydration product of Portland cement, while fundamental questions persist regarding its colloidal structure and water content. In this work, we developed a full atomistic C-S-H colloid model and investigated the physical and mechanical properties at different gel water concentrations. Water confined in nanometer gel pores degrades the mechanical properties of C-S-H because of its hydrolysis effect. A “ductile to brittle” transition was observed in the C-S-H colloid model with increasing gel water contents, evolving from transgranular failure to intergranular fracture. The gel water confined in nanometer-sized pores displays glassy characteristics, and it acts as a lubricant and facilitates structure distortions. We elucidated the topology effect of the hydrogen bond network on the evolution of the viscoelasticity of C-S-H at different humidities. This work sheds light on the role of water in C-S-H colloids from nanostructure perspectives. Keywords: C-S-H; Atomistic simulation; Colloid model; Humidity; Gel water; Molecular dynamics; Mechanical property

1. Introduction Calcium silicate hydrate (C-S-H), the most significant binding component in concrete, is the dominant product in cement hydration. However, C-S-H remains one of the most “controversial” materials because of its complex and diverse microstructure and morphology. It is considered a short-range ordered but longrange disordered quasi-crystalline material with a localized microstructure akin to tobermorite [1]. Foil-like morphology is typical in C-S-H gel [2], especially at high water to solid ratios in cement hydration [3]. The C-S-H foils fold and curl into wrinkled structures, forming the silicate network (Figure 1A). From the morphological microstructure perspective, Jennings proposed a C-S-H colloidal model (CM-I) based on the hierarchical packing of C-S-H globules [4]. The modified colloid model II (CM-II) [5] described that the C-S-H layered blocks are less than 5 nm, and there exist different kinds of pores due to various packing density, which composes 2-4 Å interlayer spacing, <3 nm small gel pores and large gel pores from 3 to 12 nm. The CM-II colloid model successfully interpreted the microstructure change during hydration, including the gel pore structure evolution. Although these models can be applied to practical issues such as drying or autogenous shrinkage, they cannot quantitatively evaluate the microstructure. For example, one currently unsolved question is how nanosized gel pore structure and gel water concentration affect the bulk properties? The emergence of C-S-H atomistic models offers possibilities to establish quantitative relationships between the microstructure and mechanical properties. The classical C-S-H model proposed by Pellenq et al. [5] illustrated the effect of interlayer water on C-S-H properties like stiffness and strength. It is noteworthy that the atomistic structures of C-S-H have been greatly enriched through combinatorial molecular optimizations [6]. By deciphering the chemical order/ disorder of C-S-H, it helps to interpret the experimental results and provide theoretical insights into understanding the structural and dynamic properties of C- S-H [7–10]. These works inspired researchers to unveil the interplays between water and the C-S-H gel at different length scales. For example, the water confined in the interlayer space adopts a unique multirange structure with distorted tetrahedral coordination at a short range up to 2.7 Å  [11]. The motion of gel water in slit geometry pores has been extensively investigated taking into account of influences of temperature [12,13], pressure [14], and foreign ions [15]. Note that the interparticle interactions in the aqueous C-S-H colloidal system have been established, which paves the way for developing realistic mesoscale models [16]. Such models at mesoscale have the advantage of investigating the texture

Enlightened by the CM-II model, in this work, we developed a full atomistic C-S- H colloid model through random packing of C-S-H unit cell blocks and subsequent structural optimization. The dimension of the C-S-H unit block was controlled as 20.8×36.5×44.0 Å to match the unit size by X-ray [23] and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) [24] measurements (Figure 1B) that each C-S-H block possesses 4 layers at ~5 nm. Then six identical C-S-H unit blocks (same size and composition) were packed inside the simulation supercell to construct the C-S-H colloid particle model that is based and conformed with CM-II model at a total size of 6nm3-8nm3. Moreover, the blocks were randomly packed together at controlled orientations as the initial structure, as illustrated in Figure 1C. An order parameter, S, was defined for structure comparisons. The remaining space (less than 3 nm channels) between C-S-H particles can be filled by water molecules using the grand canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) technique at desirable concentrations. After a sufficient structural optimization, a 3 ns equilibrium run in this work, different models with various water contents can be constructed (Figure 1D). The final colloid model is about 6.5 nm in diameter that is consistent with the concept of “globule floc” proposed by Jennings [4] with the size, unit block numbers, and morphology highly comparable, and it is further refined and validated with experiments. We investigated the mechanical properties of the C-S-H colloidal models through the molecular dynamics simulation by employing uniaxial compression, tension, and nanoindentation. Water molecules confined in nanometer gel pores exhibit vitreous characteristics, leading to strength degradation due to hydrolysis. We revealed that the well-structured hydrogen bond network dominates the mechanical properties at the nanoscale, which could be the underlying mechanism to the viscoelasticity of C-S-H. This work provides nanoscale insights into the roles of water bounded in gel pores, and it opens new ways in relating the gel water to the cohesion of the C-S-H gel, the mechanical properties, and the durability of cement-based materials. 2. A significant negative correlation between porosity and water content is observed, while the density of C-S-H colloids is uncorrelated with the water concentration, which indicates the structural integrity of the C-S-H colloid model. The random packing and structure relaxation process can homogenize the system by rearranging the atoms, leading to relatively isotropic mechanical properties, providing new insights into the experiments. Herein, the dry colloid model without gel water exhibits low friction but strong cohesion. The adsorption of water in saturated structures induces heterogenous fillings in gel pores, leading to lower friction between two adjacent surfaces. 11% RH, 30% gel water content shown in this work is a critical point for the monolayer water film on the C-S-H surface, implying the exposed C-S-H surfaces are nearly covered with water molecules. Conclusions A full atomistic C-S-H colloid model was developed through the random packing strategy, and it was thoroughly explored and examined at different gel water concentrations. The proposed full-atomistic C-S-H colloid model exhibits better isotropic features involving different mechanical properties than the single unit block C-S-H model because of its uniform arrangement of atoms. The physical and mechanical properties were systematically investigated. This work is highlighted with the novel insights on the effects of water concentration on C-S-H colloid at a larger scale, and we have the following findings: (1) Water molecules tend to occupy the gel pores, giving rise to a declined porosity and a smaller specific surface area. (2) Gel water in C-S-H colloid models degrades the compressive strength and tensile strength and as it acts as a lubricant and facilitates the distortion. During the deformation, some distinctive periods in terms of surface reconstruction, necking, plane slip, pore propagation can be distinguished, reflecting the “ductile to brittle” transition. (3) C-S-H colloid displays viscoelastic characteristics, and nanosized gel water is like glassy water with a higher viscosity and a bigger average H-bond number. The evolution of nanoindentation at different water concentrations is related to

# Abstract

In this paper, a support vector machine (SVM) model which can be used to predict the compressive strength of mortars exposed to sulfate attack was established. An accelerated corrosion test was applied to collect compressive strength data. For predicting the compressive strength of mortars, a total of 638 data samples obtained from experiment was chosen as a dataset to establish a SVM model. The values of the coefficient of determination, the mean absolute error, the mean absolute percentage error and the root mean square error were used for evaluating the predictive accuracy. The main factors affecting the predicted compressive strength were obtained by sensitivity analysis. A SVM model was calibrated, validated, and finally established. Moreover, the performance of the SVM model was compared to an artificial neural network (ANN) model. Results show that the prediction values from the SVM model were close to the experimental values; the main factors sensitive to concrete compressive strength were exposure time, water-cement ratio and sulfate ions; the performance of the SVM model was better than the ANN model. The SVM model developed in this study can be potentially used for predicting the compressive strength of cement-based materials servicing in harsh environments.

## Introduction

Concrete is an important structural material being used in civil engineering and industrial facilities. The strength of concrete is considered as one of the most important property for a given concrete mix design. Besides the constituent of materials, the strength is also affected by environmental exposure and extreme working conditions [1]. In harsh environments, especially the areas with abundant sulfate ions, the properties of concrete materials can easily deteriorate, which could affect the safety of engineering structures [2]. For the safety assessment of existing structures, compressive strength is often considered as the most important indicator of concrete quality [3, 4]. Monitoring concrete strength during service can give an idea about the time for concrete quality control and performance maintenance [5]. In addition, predicting concrete strength can be helpful in assessing the deterioration of concrete structures and

Unfortunately, due to the complex degradation mechanisms and multiple influencing parameters [7], there is no effective method to predict compressive strength of cement-based materials in harsh environments. To date, there are two categories about the prediction of concrete compressive strength [8]. The first category is traditional mathematics statistical forecasting methods. It needs a huge amount of data. When the sample data tends to infinity, it tends to predict real results, but the actual number of samples is often limited. The second category, nonlinear prediction methods, lacks a unified mathematical theory. The predicted results are often a partial optimal solution, rather than a global optimal solution. For conventional concrete, the above categories can all be used to predict the values of compressive strength, but for concrete exposed to sulfate attack as the number of input factor increases, the relationship between the input factors and the compressive strength becomes highly nonlinear and complex. Hence, the regression models are not suitable for predicting the values of compressive strength of concrete in harsh environments. Therefore, more attentions have been paid to models based on artificial intelligence. Machine learning techniques, such as artificial neural network (ANN) is increasingly used to simulate the strength of concrete materials and has become an important research area [9–12]. An ANN model is usually consisted of inputs, weights, sum function, activation function and outputs. The related algorithms require setting up of different learning parameters, the optimal number of nodes in the hidden layer and the number of hidden layers. Until now, back-propagation (BP) algorithm, which adjusts connection weights and bias values during training, has been widely used for training an ANN model. However, ANN models still have disadvantages: (1) The information about the relative significance of the various parameters cannot be provided [13]; (2) A reasonable interpretation of the overall structure of the network is hard to be established [14]. In addition, ANN models have some intrinsic disadvantages such as slow convergence speed, less generalizing effectiveness, arriving at local minimum and over-fitting problems [15]. To overcome those limitations, in recent years, researchers have explored the potential of support vector machine (SVM) in performance of cement-based materials. SVM, a nonlinear modeling approach, proposed based on the statistical theory by Vapnik [16] is being applied in the field of civil engineering. Unlike ANN models, a SVM model has the advantage of reducing training error and being a unique and globally optimum [17]. The method has excellent generalization capability when solving non-linear problems. It can also overcome the problem of small sample size. For example, Yan and Shi [18] used SVM to predict the elastic modulus of normal and high strength concrete. The analytical results showed that the SVM outperformed other models. Chou et al. [19] predicted the compressive strength of high performance concrete by using the SVM technique, and the behavior simulation capability of SVM was investigated using concrete data from several countries. Cheng et al. [20] proposed an advanced hybrid AI model that fused fuzzy logic, weight SVM and fast messy genetic algorithms to predict compressive strength of concrete. Gupta [21] investigated the potential use of SVM for predicting CCS by combining radial basis function with SVM. There have been few studies on the prediction of the compressive strength of cement-based materials exposed to sulfate attack using SVM. Most of these studies established the prediction models of concrete compressive strength mainly based on the material factors (e.g., waterbinder ratio, water content and aggregate content) and curing age [9–12, 18–20]. However, for concrete subjected to service in a harsh environment, environmental factors are of great importance to the compressive strength and should be considered in the compressive strength prediction models.

## Experimental program

### 3.1 Materials

Type II ordinary Portland (P II 52.5) cement purchased from China United Cement Corporation was used in this study. The chemical composition and mineral original composition of cement are shown in Tables 1 and 2, respectively. ISO standard sand with a density of 2.58 g/ cm3 obtained from Xiamen standard sand Co., Ltd. was used as fine aggregate. The maximum sizes of the sands were 4.75 mm. A superplasticizer (SP) with 36.8 wt% solid content was purchased from Jiangsu Sobute New materials Co. Ltd. and its water-reducing ratio was 29.8%. Tap water was used in concrete mixtures and curing application in this study. Na2SO4, analytically pure, obtained from China Guoyao Chemical Company, is used to prepare different concentrations of sodium sulfate solutions.

### 3.2 Mix proportion and specimens preparation

Three types of mortar (M65, M50, M28) with respective w/c ratio of 0.65, 0.50 and 0.28 were designed and the compositions is shown in Table 3. The compressive strengths of mortars exposed to sulfate attack are shown in Fig 2. The results show that the compressive strength values of all specimens gently increased in the early stages. ## Conclusions

In this study, a prediction model of mortar compressive strength was established by SVM. A total of 638 sample data collected from the experimental test were used to develop the SVM model for predicting compressive strength. The SVM model was first calibrated and then verified using the experimental data from corroded concrete samples. Conclusions can be drawn as follows:

1. The compressive strength values of all mortar specimens increased and then decreased gradually when the specimens were degraded by sodium sulfate solutions. The experimental results show that, after degraded by the same concentration of solution, the greater the w/c ratios, the larger the descent rate of compressive strength.

2. The sensitivity analysis results show that the main factors influencing the prediction of mortar compressive strength were exposure time, w/c ratio and sulfate concentration.
